newsitem.title: MALAWI: Mozambique offers landlocked Malawi port facilities.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique offers landlocked Malawi port facilities.

text.p: Landlocked Malawi will soon begin operating direct seaport facilities on the Indian Ocean in Mozambique once details are finalised during bilateral talks set for mid-June, a government minister said on Monday.

Malawian Transport and Aviation Minister Harry Thompson told Reuters that Mozambique had offered a 51 percent concession in the activities of its northern port of Nacala to Malawi's private sector and 16 percent to the Malawi Railways. It will keep a 33 percent stake.
"The hard talking will be done in Mozambique. In two weeks' time I will be leading a business delegation to Maputo," he said in an interview.
"Once the proper deal is signed, we'll build our offices at the port," he added.
Thompson said the 51 percent interest would be open to Malawi's clearing and forwarding agents, tea and tobacco exporters and others.

The minister said he could not say how much Malawi planned to invest in the new offer until the deal was finalised but added that Malawi was considering making a reciprocal concession offer to Mozambique.
"Malawi has to look at a similar offer," he said, without giving details.
Malawi's main route to the seaport for many years was through Mozambique's 800km-long Nacala rail line, 200km of which is inside Malawi.

But the 16-year-old civil war in Mozambique, which kept the rail line under constant disruption, forced Malawi to use road freight through the country's three outlets of Mwanza to Zimbabwe, Mchinji to Zambia and Kaporo to Tanzania.

Business on the Nacala rail line began to pick up after a peace agreement was signed in Mozambique in 1992 followed by democratic elections in 1994. Cargo movement rose to 120,000 tonnes in 1996 from 112,640 tonnes in 1995.
